🔐 ⚠️ phpMyAdmin 5.2.3 - 2FA Bypass! 0day++! ⚠️ 🔐 

🚨 WebAuthn signatures are parsed but never COSE-verified against credentialPublicKey 🚨 Arbitrary bytes pass the structural checks, so 2FA falls over after password auth 💀

Exploit:
> CWE-347/287 ⚠️ CVSS 8.1
> 🐙 https://t.co/ma6OkI0sOF

🧩 Root cause: web-auth/webauthn-lib is only a dev/suggest dependency 📦 The distributed tarball is built with `composer install --no-dev`, so `WebAuthn::createServer` instantiates `CustomServer` instead of `WebauthnLibServer` 👀

🔍 How? 🤦‍♂️ `CustomServer::parseAndValidateAssertionResponse` enforces structural checks only: clientData type, session challenge, origin host, rpIdHash, user-present, allowed credential id 📋 `response.signature` is decoded and never verified ❌ `credentialPublicKey` is never read 🕳️

💥 Impact: a well-formed assertion carrying correct structural fields and an arbitrary signature yields a full authenticated session 🔓 Impact is unauthorized database access through the application, not host-level code execution 🗄️

RT @cyb3rops: I actually expect AI to make software considerably more secure in the coming years. Obvious coding mistakes will become harder to find, and exploiting software vulnerabilities may become much more difficult than it is today.

But you don’t need to discover a new software vulnerability to compromise most organizations.

Stolen or reused credentials, phishing, session hijacking, social engineering that tricks people into executing malicious code, compromised software suppliers, trojanized applications, malicious updates, insecure configurations, exposed secrets and backups, excessive privileges, abused remote management tools, and weaknesses in authentication and business processes.

There are plenty of ways into an organization that don’t require developing an exploit or discovering a new vulnerability.

And AI agents can automate and combine these methods just as effectively. They can test different approaches, adapt when something fails, and work their way towards the objective.

That’s what this post was about.

- TLS traffic over DHE ciphers have a 1-byte secret, "04", meaning anyone can decrypt connections to these devices and steal login credentials and session tokens if the client negotiated with DHE ciphers like the latest TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, which is extremely likely.

RT @zoecyber001: When you shut down a modern iPhone, the Power Management Unit (PMU) cuts voltage to the main A-series processor, the OLED display, and the camera array. It leaves a separate Low Power Mode (LPM) rail live on the motherboard.

Sitting on that energized rail are three wireless chips: the Bluetooth controller, the NXP NFC controller, and the Apple U1 Ultra-Wideband chip.

Apple built this hardware partition to run "Findable After Power Off," Express Transit passes, and Digital Car Keys when your battery dies. Even with iOS completely unloaded from RAM, those three chips stay powered for up to 24 hours on a manual shutdown (and up to 5 hours on automatic battery reserve).

Right before iOS powers down, it pre-computes 96 rolling NIST P-224 public keys (one for every 15-minute window over the next 24 hours) and sends them to the Bluetooth chip using Host Controller Interface (HCI) commands.

The final HCI command severs communication with the main processor and starts a standalone thread inside the Bluetooth silicon. While the main SoC sits unpowered, the Bluetooth chip wakes up every 2 seconds to broadcast the current P-224 public key over Bluetooth Low Energy. Any passing iPhone or MacBook that hears that broadcast encrypts its own GPS coordinates with your broadcasted public key and relays the packet to Apple servers.

In 2022, researchers at the SEEMOO lab at TU Darmstadt audited this low-power hardware chain ("Evil Never Sleeps") and found a major gap between the three wireless chips.

While the NFC chip runs encrypted and signed firmware and the U1 Ultra-Wideband chip checks cryptographic signatures at boot, the Broadcom Bluetooth chip has neither encryption nor signature verification on its firmware updates.

Broadcom bakes its base Bluetooth firmware into read-only Mask ROM at the factory. To fix bugs and load the standalone Find My feature, iOS writes raw binary patches directly into the chip internal SRAM using a mechanism called PatchRAM (Write_RAM HCI commands). The hardware never checks a cryptographic signature on those RAM patches.

If an attacker already has kernel-level code execution on iOS (through spyware or a local jailbreak exploit), they can overwrite the Bluetooth chip PatchRAM in SRAM before the user powers the phone down.

When the user drags the power-off slider, iOS halts and wipes main system RAM. Because the PMU keeps the LPM power rail alive, the modified Bluetooth firmware stays in SRAM and keeps executing on reserve battery power.

Yeah, I mean zero-days always sound cool, but hacking large organisations with mature SOC and detection engineering teams, while maintaining operational security, applying good tradecraft, evading controls, and avoiding high-confidence alerts is an underrated skill that a lot of people do not fully understand.

The difficulty comes from the breadth of skills involved. Real adversary simulation is not just Windows internals, payload development, or solving a CTF-style lab. It is also not 'please install my game cheat after disabling every security protection so I only have to evade one anti-cheat process.'

In a real environment you may need to work around layers like:

1. Email security and phishing controls
2. Web proxies and URL filtering
3. EDR and antivirus
4. AppLocker / WDAC
5. IDS / IPS
6. Firewalls and network segmentation
7. MFA and Conditional Access
8. Identity providers and SSO
9. AD internals, Kerberos, LDAP and delegation
10. PAM / privileged access controls
11. Cloud controls and IAM
12. DLP
13. SIEM ingestion and custom detections
14. Behavioural analytics
15. Threat hunting
16. SOC playbooks and incident response
17. Endpoint, network, identity and cloud telemetry

etc...

And you have to understand the blue-team side well enough to know what telemetry your actions create, what actually gets ingested, what rules are likely to fire, what looks normal in that specific environment, and how defenders will investigate what you leave behind.

That is where OPSEC, evasion and tradecraft become much more complicated. It is not just 'does my payload bypass Defender?' It is whether your entire operation makes sense against that organisation's controls, people, architecture and detection capability.

I think part of the misunderstanding comes from people judging red teaming based on the cringe stuff they see on Twitter, and honestly I do not blame them.

Having spent time on both the game-hacking side and the red/blue-team side, there is definitely crossover, but there are also skills missing on both sides that neither always fully appreciates.

It should not even be 'this side vs that side.' The more you understand about computers, operating systems, networking, exploitation, identity, cloud, detection engineering, malware, reverse engineering, tradecraft and how real environments operate, the better hacker you become overall.

Being a specialist in one tiny area does not mean everyone outside that area sucks. You never really know what someone else knows or has done.

Ego and arrogance just get in the way of learning.

quotedTweet.rawContent:
Preliminary result of my "realistic traffic" php2shell benchmark with `nginx -> Apache (15 workers) + mod_php` and PHP 8.4.26.

This setup is interesting, because reverse-proxies are common, and you cannot control the worker you are going to reach.

- Blue: success rate of the memory leak.
- Red: success rate of command execution.
- x-axis: requests/s benign traffic in parallel 

Everything is default config, except Apache with 15 workers (default 150). I lowered it, because I wanted it to be easier to saturate the workers with the traffic. 
With 100req/s traffic on 150 workers, the exploit still had 100% success rate. With 15 workers, it starts to drop to 94%.

Traffic is being generated on the host itself directly, to avoid it looking like a DoS attempt over the network. But the exploit is being executed on my laptop to the remote host, so we don't have any advantage with low ping (we need to wait for the cookie leak, before sending the next stage).

The exploit uses a fanout strategy, throwing 15 requests per stage (so 60 in total). For 150 workers it would be 600 requests.

But I wouldn't call it suitable for blind black-box testing. I ran 14,877 fresh exploit attempts - every ARM target against every ARM and x86 profile, each in a fresh lab. Wrong profiles are destructive: 58.3% crashed the lab (56.4% ARM profiles, 60.2% x86 profiles replayed on ARM). And HTTP-only fingerprinting was useless: all 87 builds returned byte-identical responses, so you cannot safely guess the profile without force/out-of-band info. Bug bounty hunters, please do not spray profiles at production :)

Nine years ago, when I started my career as a Node.js SWE, I never imagined that an ordinary body-parser setup on a Node.js runtime could become an RCE entry point.

2026 keeps surprising me. And it's making me look at attack surfaces differently...

Huge respect to the researchers who found this bug

Announcing 3 Critical vulns for hundreds of millions of IoT, Firewalls, OT, and Military devices including: Palo Alto Networks, Comcast, D-Link, HP, Canon, Honeywell, GE, Oracle, Siemens, Rockwell, Digi, Lockheed Martin, Boeing... 

The vulns are with GoAhead Web Server which is a backend library used by these devices. There's a patch available from GoAhead but that doesn't mean there's a patch available for the devices yet -- that's up to the manufacturer.

- TLS traffic over DHE ciphers have a 1-byte secret, "04", meaning anyone can decrypt connections to these devices and steal login credentials and session tokens if the client negotiated with DHE ciphers like the latest TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, which is extremely likely.

- LibreSSL mTLS has been completely bypassed, meaning anyone can connect over mTLS. If you have one of these devices listening on the internet and are expecting mTLS to protect it from attackers, take it offline or patch asap.

- OpenSSL Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) are not enforced, meaning if a user device is stolen or compromised, and you revoke that mTLS cert, nothing actually happens. There are a lot of other attacks this can be used for.

These are critical because these types of devices run our world. Water systems, electricity, military, firewalls, critical infrastructure.

The vulns are with GoAhead Web Server which is a backend library used by these devices. There's a patch available from GoAhead but that doesn't mean there's a patch available for the devices yet -- that's up to the manufacturer.

- TLS traffic over DHE ciphers have a 1-byte secret, "04", meaning anyone can decrypt connections to these devices and steal login credentials and session tokens if the client negotiated with DHE ciphers like the latest TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, which is extremely likely.

- OpenSSL Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) are not enforced, meaning if a user device is stolen or compromised, and you revoke that mTLS cert, nothing actually happens. There are a lot of other attacks this can be used for.

These are critical because these types of devices run our world. Water systems, electricity, military, firewalls, critical infrastructure.

Growing up with financial struggles, in a village or town, with mostly regional-language education shaped my confidence. My school called itself English medium, but hardly anyone taught in English.

My parents worked hard to support me. But I was also taught not to question them or any elder, teacher, police officer, rich person, or city person. I grew up feeling like I should always obey and never speak up.

That followed me into engineering and work. Struggling to express myself, stumbling over words during presentations, sweating, finding it hard to say no. Being the obedient “nice guy” comes at a cost.

Many people around the world grow up this way, constantly worrying about how others see them, afraid of humiliation or awkwardness, and holding themselves back from taking risks.

I’m learning to push myself out of my comfort zone, speak up, and stand up for myself. It’s okay to express your thoughts and clarify what you mean when someone misunderstands you. You don’t have to silently accept their version of you.

Let yourself be awkward while you practise. Trust me, people care far less about your awkward moments than you think. They have their own lives and worries.

That’s how you grow and build confidence. With practice, you can communicate more clearly, feel more comfortable during presentations, and perform better at work. You don’t have to keep holding yourself back.

Ask questions. Say no. Make mistakes. Express yourself. Just be mindful of your words and be kind.
